tools.what_it_times: send to receive (end to end), and separately send to got-it (publish latency)

clock_and_resolution.finding: Two clocks. Publish latency uses System.nanoTime() inside one JVM, recorded in microseconds into an HdrHistogram at 5 significant digits. End-to-end latency uses wall clocks on two machines: the consumer takes System.currentTimeMillis() and subtracts a publish timestamp, the subtraction is done in WHOLE MILLISECONDS and only then multiplied into microseconds. Every end-to-end value is therefore an exact multiple of 1000 microseconds: the microsecond unit and the 5-digit precision are nominal, and the real granularity is 1 ms. The publish timestamp is not always the benchmark's own: the Kafka driver passes the broker's record timestamp and the Pulsar driver the broker's publish time, while NATS, Pravega, JMS and Artemis stamp it in the producer.

odd_values.finding: End-to-end values of zero or below are silently dropped: `if (endToEndLatencyMicros > 0)` gates all three end-to-end sinks. They are not counted anywhere and nothing is logged, while the message still increments messagesReceived, so the message count and the latency sample count diverge with no indicator. Because the value is millisecond-granular, this drops not only clock-skew negatives but EVERY delivery faster than a millisecond, which computes as exactly zero: the tool cannot report a sub-millisecond end-to-end latency at all, and the fastest messages are the ones excluded. On the publish side there is no lower guard, only an upper clamp recording anything above 60 s as exactly 60 s.

warnings.finding: None in the repository or the official documentation. README.md does not contain the word 'latency'; no markdown file mentions CPU contention or co-location. The docs page defines publish latency and publish delay and says values over 60 s 'are not captured', which the code contradicts: it records them as exactly 60 s, so maxima and high percentiles saturate rather than being absent. The docs do not define end-to-end latency at all and give no clock or NTP caveat. The only mitigation in the repository is silent: the Kafka ansible deployment installs chrony on the client hosts. The nearest thing to a warning is in the issue tracker, where a maintainer writes that end-to-end latency uses timestamps from different nodes and is 'really not super-reliable'.

tools.what_it_times: send to receive; separately publish to broker confirm (send to got-it), both stamped in one JVM

clock_and_resolution.finding: The clock is chosen at runtime: System.nanoTime() by default, System.currentTimeMillis() when --use-millis is passed, which the documentation prescribes for producer and consumer on different machines. Latency is collected in ns or ms but reported in microseconds by integer division by 1000, which truncates toward zero, so any sub-microsecond latency prints as 0. The tool does not use HdrHistogram: percentiles come from a Dropwizard ExponentiallyDecayingReservoir, a 1028-element decaying random sample biased to the last five minutes, not from every recorded value.

odd_values.finding: Negative latencies are silently turned positive, not dropped and not kept: getDifference returns Math.abs(ts1 - ts2). Under --use-millis, the documented cross-machine mode, a consumer clock behind the producer's reports the magnitude of the clock offset AS LATENCY, with no sign check, no counter and no warning. A missing or unparseable timestamp is signalled by a sentinel for which the method returns -1, which the consumed path filters with `if (latency >= 0)`; a genuine zero latency is therefore kept. The confirm path filters nothing at all. Nothing crashes.

warnings.finding: On clock synchronisation the documentation is explicit: the machines 'should have their clock synchronised, e.g. by NTP', with the explanation that nanoTime must be used only within one JVM. Beyond that, nothing: no warning about thread scheduling, CPU contention, coordinated omission, or what residual error an NTP-synchronised pair leaves, and no hint that the absolute value masks a backwards clock. The only admonition in the whole document set is an unrelated deprecation notice.

tools.audit_found: it does not keep negatives: Math.abs turns them into positive latencies of the same size, so a clock offset is reported as delay and cannot be told from one

tools.what_it_times: nats latency: send to receive. nats bench: varies by mode, and on core NATS publish it times only the local enqueue call, not a trip

clock_and_resolution.finding: The two commands use different clocks. `nats latency` is wall-clock and non-monotonic: the publisher writes time.Now().UnixNano() into the payload and the subscriber subtracts it from its own, and calling UnixNano strips Go's monotonic reading, so an NTP step during a run lands directly in the sample. Both connections are opened by the same process on one host, so the exposure is that one clock moving, not cross-machine skew. `nats bench` uses time.Since, which keeps the monotonic reading and cannot go backwards. Percentiles in `nats latency` come from an HdrHistogram whose upper bound is taken from the data after sorting.

odd_values.finding: `nats latency` drops out-of-range values from the histogram while keeping them in the headline statistics, so the two outputs can disagree. RecordValue is called with its error return ignored, and the histogram library rejects a negative value; but the value stays in the slice that prints Minimum, Median and Maximum Latency and the raw dump. A backwards clock step would therefore print a negative minimum while the percentile table silently ignores it. `nats bench` casts a duration to unsigned, which would wrap a negative rather than reject it, though its monotonic clock makes that unreachable. Neither has a sign check, a zero check, a counter or a warning, and neither crashes.

tools.audit_found: keeps them in the printed minimum, median and maximum, but the histogram silently refuses them, so the percentile table and the headline numbers can disagree
